title: All shall be well
hook: Julian heard: all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well (Revelations 27)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hazelnut: all creation in Julian's palm. Your line was it lasts because it's loved. Did your pocket remind you? Day two hundred seventy-three, the end of the week.

It's the question everyone eventually asks. Usually at night, usually after bad news. A diagnosis. A child in trouble. A headline you can't stop thinking about. If God is good, why is there so much wrong in the world? Why didn't God just prevent it? Julian of Norwich asked exactly that. Not as a debate, but as someone who had lived through plague. She says she wondered why, in God's great wisdom, sin hadn't simply been stopped at the start. And the answer she received has become one of the most quoted lines in English. Today: all shall be well.
screen: `THE QUESTION AT NIGHT.` → `WHY NOT PREVENT IT?` → `JULIAN ASKED IT TOO.`

segments.voice: It's in chapter twenty-seven of her book. Julian thinks, as many of us would, that if only there had never been sin, everything would have been fine. Why allow it? And she hears Jesus answer. First, a strange phrase: sin is behovable, an old word meaning something like fitting, or bound to be. Scholars still discuss exactly what she meant. And then, in Grace Warrack's 1901 version, the famous words: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Notice what the answer doesn't do. It doesn't explain the suffering. It doesn't say the pain isn't real, or that it's secretly good. Julian says plainly that she didn't understand how it could be true. She saw the evil in the world clearly. She even says, later on, that God will do a great deed at the end of time, and that we can't know now what it is or how it will make everything well. So this isn't optimism. Optimism says things will probably work out. Julian's line is stranger and stronger. It says: even the things that won't work out are held inside a love bigger than they are. That's why it's said three times, like a heartbeat. All shall be well. And all shall be well. And all manner of thing, every kind of thing, shall be well. Six hundred years later, the poet T. S. Eliot wove her words into one of his most famous poems. Look back at this week: Hildegard's greening, Bernard's four loves, Francis's family of creatures, the cloud, Julian's cell, her hazelnut. Every one of them was reaching for this: love underneath everything.
screen: `WHY NOT PREVENT SIN?` · `SIN IS BEHOVABLE.` · `ALL SHALL BE WELL.` · `NOT OPTIMISM: HELD IN LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it once, slowly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing that is not well right now. Don't push it away. Hold it honestly. Then, slowly, say Julian's words, aloud or silently: all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well. Don't force yourself to feel it. Just let the words sit next to the thing that hurts. The bell holds the time.
All shall be well. Julian's answer to why: not an explanation, but a promise that all is held in love.
Your line: all shall be well. Today, when bad news comes, big or small, say it once under your breath, next to the worry, not instead of it. Day two hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Many Christians repeat Julian's words in times of grief or fear, and her line is often read at funerals, printed on cards, and prayed slowly as a single sentence.

fork.setup: you're Julian. you've asked why God didn't simply prevent sin. what kind of answer comes?
options: a promise: all shall be well.
fork.reveal: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." a promise, not an explanation.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cheerful don't-worry line.
what it means: evil is real, and not explained; but all things are held in a love that will make them well.
what a scholar hears: chapter 27's 'sin is behovable'; the 'great deed' of chapter 32; and Eliot's use of the line in Little Gidding (1942).
